alternatives.label: Later chronology (Philistine pressure in the 11th century)

gifts.name: Discerning that the LORD was calling Samuel

events.title: Mistakes Hannah's prayer for drunkenness, then blesses her
events.summary: Eli sees Hannah's lips moving silently at the Shiloh sanctuary, rebukes her as drunk, then hears her explanation and prays that God grant her request.

events.title: Fails to restrain his sons
events.summary: Hophni and Phinehas take sacrificial meat by force and lie with women serving at the sanctuary; Eli rebukes them mildly but does not remove them.

events.title: Oracle against Eli's house
events.summary: An unnamed man of God announces that Eli's priestly line will be cut off and replaced by a faithful priest; 1 Kings sees the fulfilment in Solomon's removal of Abiathar.

events.title: Teaches Samuel to answer the call
events.summary: Realising the LORD is calling the boy, Eli tells Samuel to say, Speak, for your servant hears, and then accepts the hard message against his own house.

events.title: Dies at the news of the ark's capture
events.summary: Ninety-eight, blind and heavy, Eli falls backward and breaks his neck when told that Israel was routed, his sons killed and the ark taken by the Philistines.

summary: Eli was the aged priest at Shiloh at the end of the period of the judges, the man who first misjudged and then blessed Hannah and who raised Samuel in the sanctuary. The text credits him with judging Israel forty years, but its portrait is dominated by his failure to restrain his corrupt sons Hophni and Phinehas, which brings a prophetic sentence on his priestly house. He dies on hearing that the ark of God has been captured.
textSays: Priest at Shiloh who judged Israel forty years (1 Sam 4:18). His sons abused their office and he honoured them above God (1 Sam 2:29). A man of God and then Samuel announced judgment on his house. He died at ninety-eight when the ark was captured.

interpretations.view: Rabbinic readings often treat Eli sympathetically as a righteous but indulgent father; his acceptance of judgment ('It is the LORD; let him do what seems good to him') is admired.
Eli is commonly used as a cautionary example for leaders who tolerate sin in their own households, and as a model of a mentor who points a younger person to God's voice.

context: Shiloh housed the tabernacle and ark in the late judges period. Its destruction is not narrated in Samuel but is recalled in Ps 78:60 and Jer 7:12-14; archaeological evidence for an 11th-century destruction at Shiloh is debated.
legacy: His line continued through Ahimelech and Abiathar until Solomon removed Abiathar, which 1 Kings presents as fulfilment of the oracle against Eli's house.
voice: Old, weary and gentle; speaks slowly, is quick to bless, slow to confront, and resigned before God's verdict.

events.title: Barren and provoked by a rival wife
events.summary: Hannah is one of Elkanah's two wives. He loves her and gives her a double portion, but Peninnah, who has children, provokes her year after year at the Shiloh feast.

events.title: Vows a son to the LORD
events.summary: In deep distress she prays at the sanctuary and vows that if God gives her a son he will be given to the LORD all his life, and no razor will touch his head.

events.title: Misjudged by Eli, then blessed
events.summary: Eli thinks her silent praying is drunkenness. She explains she has been pouring out her soul; he blesses her, and she goes away no longer downcast.

events.title: Birth and naming of Samuel
events.summary: The LORD remembers her; she conceives and names the boy Samuel, explaining that she asked him of the LORD.

events.title: Presents Samuel at Shiloh
events.summary: After weaning him she brings Samuel with offerings to Eli and lends him to the LORD for life, fulfilling her vow.

events.title: Song of Hannah
events.summary: She sings of a God who reverses fortunes, lifting the poor and humbling the proud, and ends by speaking of the LORD's king and anointed before Israel has a king.

events.title: Yearly robe and further children
events.summary: Each year she makes Samuel a little robe; Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah, and she bears three more sons and two daughters.

journey.note: Home of Elkanah in the hill country of Ephraim (Ramathaim-zophim).
Annual pilgrimage to the sanctuary; her vow and prayer.
Returns home; Samuel is born.
Brings the weaned Samuel to Eli and sings her song.
Returns home, visiting Samuel yearly.

summary:
Hannah is the woman whose anguished prayer opens the books of Samuel. Childless and mocked by her husband's other wife, she pours out her grief at the Shiloh sanctuary and vows to give a son back to the LORD. God answers, and she hands the young Samuel over to Eli to serve at the sanctuary for life.

Her song (1 Sam 2:1-10) is one of the theological keys to the books that follow. It celebrates a God who brings low and raises up, who feeds the hungry and empties the full, and it ends with the first mention in Samuel of the LORD's king, his anointed one. The reversals she sings about play out in the stories of Eli and Samuel, Saul and David.

She is also an example of honest prayer: she does not hide her bitterness, she persists year after year, and she keeps a costly vow once her prayer is answered.
textSays: Wife of Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim; barren while Peninnah had children (1 Sam 1:2). She prayed silently at Shiloh, vowed her son to the LORD, bore Samuel, gave him to Eli once he was weaned, and sang a prayer (1 Sam 2:1-10). Afterwards she bore three sons and two daughters (1 Sam 2:21).

interpretations.view: The Talmud (Berakhot 31a-b) derives rules for the Amidah prayer from Hannah: praying with directed heart, moving the lips while keeping the voice inaudible. Her story is read as the haftarah on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, linked with the idea that God remembers the barren on that day.
Hannah is read as a type of Mary; the Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55) closely echoes her song. Orthodox liturgy uses the Song of Hannah among the biblical odes sung at Matins.
Hannah is often held up as a model of persistent, honest prayer and of entrusting children to God, and her song as a summary of God's preference for the humble.

Many scholars think the song was an older royal psalm placed in Hannah's mouth by the editor, noting its reference to a king (1 Sam 2:10); others argue it fits its setting as anticipatory prophecy. Both views agree it frames the book's theme of reversal.

strengths: Brings real grief to God instead of hiding it
Theological depth: her song anticipates the monarchy
failures: The text records no notable failure; she is portrayed as wholly sympathetic

context: Barrenness carried real social shame and economic risk in Israelite society. Polygamy, as in Elkanah's household, is described without endorsement and, as with Sarah and Hagar or Rachel and Leah, produces rivalry. The Nazirite-like vow (no razor) recalls Samson (Judg 13:5).
legacy: Her song is echoed in Mary's Magnificat and in Christian and Jewish liturgy. She stands in the line of barren mothers through whom God gives a key child: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson's mother, Elizabeth.

traditions.text: Rabbinic tradition counts Hannah among the seven women prophets of Israel.

voice: Quiet but intense; speaks plainly about her sorrow, then breaks into confident, poetic praise full of contrasts between the mighty and the lowly.

names.meaning: Name of God, or Heard of God (the text links it to 'asked')

tribe: Debated: Ephraim (1 Sam 1:1) or Levi (1 Chr 6:28)

gifts.name: Prophecy: none of his words fell to the ground

events.title: Dedicated at Shiloh
events.summary: Given by Hannah to serve under Eli, the boy ministers before the LORD wearing a linen ephod.

events.title: The LORD calls Samuel
events.summary: In a time when the word of the LORD was rare, God calls the boy by name; his first message is judgment on Eli's house. All Israel comes to recognise him as a prophet.

events.title: Victory at Mizpah and Ebenezer
events.summary: Samuel calls Israel to put away foreign gods, intercedes and offers sacrifice; the LORD thunders against the Philistines. He sets up a stone called Ebenezer, 'thus far the LORD has helped us'.

events.title: Judges Israel on circuit
events.summary: Each year he travels from Ramah to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, judging Israel, and builds an altar at home in Ramah.

events.title: Israel demands a king
events.summary: His sons take bribes, and the elders ask for a king like the nations. Samuel is displeased; God tells him the people have rejected God, not Samuel, and has him warn them of what a king will take.

events.title: Anoints Saul
events.summary: Guided by God, he privately anoints Saul as leader, then presents him publicly at Mizpah by lot and writes down the rights and duties of the kingship.

events.title: Farewell address
events.summary: He defends his integrity, rehearses God's saving acts, calls down thunder in the wheat harvest, and promises not to stop praying for Israel.

events.title: Rebukes and rejects Saul
events.summary: Saul offers sacrifice without waiting and later spares Agag and the best of Amalek's livestock. Samuel declares that obedience is better than sacrifice and that God has rejected Saul as king.

events.title: Anoints David
events.summary: Sent to Jesse's house, he learns that the LORD looks on the heart, and anoints the youngest son, David.

events.title: Shelters David at Ramah
events.summary: David flees to Samuel at Naioth in Ramah; Saul's messengers and Saul himself are overcome by prophetic frenzy.

events.title: Death and mourning
events.summary: All Israel mourns him and buries him at his house in Ramah.

events.title: Appears to Saul at Endor
events.summary: Summoned by a medium at Saul's request, Samuel (or an apparition) tells Saul that he and his sons will die the next day.

journey.note: Born to Elkanah and Hannah.
Raised at the sanctuary under Eli; his call.
Assembly, repentance and victory over the Philistines.
Part of his annual judging circuit.
Circuit stop; renewal of the kingdom and confrontation with Saul.
Anoints David.
Home base; death and burial.

summary:
Samuel is the hinge figure between the judges and the kings. Given to God by his mother Hannah and raised at the Shiloh sanctuary, he is called as a boy at a time when the word of the LORD was rare, and grows into a prophet whose words do not fall to the ground. He combines roles no one else in Israel quite holds together: prophet, judge, intercessor and, in practice, priest.

When the elders demand a king like the nations, Samuel resists, warns them of the cost, and then obeys God by anointing Saul. When Saul disobeys, Samuel announces his rejection and secretly anoints David, the youngest son of Jesse. He spends the rest of his life grieving over Saul while shielding David.

Later biblical writers remember him chiefly as a man of prayer: Jeremiah pairs him with Moses as Israel's great intercessors, and the New Testament treats him as the first of the prophets after Moses.
textSays: Son of Elkanah and Hannah, dedicated from birth and raised at Shiloh (1 Sam 1-2). Called by God (1 Sam 3), judged Israel all his life on a circuit from Ramah (1 Sam 7:15-17), anointed Saul (1 Sam 10:1) and then David (1 Sam 16:13). 1 Chronicles places him in a Levitical genealogy (1 Chr 6:28) and credits him with records of David's reign (1 Chr 29:29). Acts calls him the start of the prophets (Acts 3:24).

interpretations.view: Samuel is ranked alongside Moses and Aaron (Ps 99:6). The Talmud credits him with writing the books of Judges, Ruth and his own book (completed by Gad and Nathan). Some rabbinic readings understand him as a lifelong Nazirite.

Honoured as a prophet and saint (feast 20 August). His call is read as a model of vocation and listening ('Speak, for your servant hears'), and his anointing of David as pointing to Christ the Anointed.

Emphasis falls on Samuel as faithful intercessor and on the theology of the monarchy: the request for a king was sinful in its motive, yet God used kingship for his purposes, leading to David and the messianic line.

Many scholars see in 1 Sam 8-12 a blend of pro-monarchic and anti-monarchic sources, explaining Samuel's mixed response to kingship; others read the tension as deliberate narrative ambivalence rather than source seams.

strengths: Integrity in office; no one could charge him with fraud (1 Sam 12:3-5)
Willingness to deliver hard words, even to his own mentor and to the king
failures: Appointed his sons as judges though they took bribes (1 Sam 8:1-3)
Initially judged by appearance when choosing a king (1 Sam 16:6-7)
turningPoints: The people's demand for a king (1 Sam 8)

context: Samuel's career coincides with Philistine expansion into the highlands after the loss of the ark (1 Sam 4). Israel was a tribal federation without central government, and the pressure of a militarily organised enemy is the background to the demand for a king.
legacy: Samuel defined the prophet's role in Israel's monarchy as one who anoints and also confronts kings, a pattern followed by Nathan, Elijah and others. Two biblical books bear his name, and Hebrews lists him among the heroes of faith (Heb 11:32).

traditions.text: Samuel wrote the books of Judges, Ruth and the book bearing his name; Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet completed it.
A site at Nebi Samwil, north-west of Jerusalem, has been venerated as Samuel's tomb since at least the Byzantine period.
traditions.source: Byzantine and medieval pilgrim accounts (dating debated)

voice: Grave, formal and principled; speaks with the authority of someone who has heard God since childhood, alternating between stern rebuke and genuine grief.

alternatives.label: Short-reign reconstructions (2 or so years, reading 1 Sam 13:1 literally)

skills.name: Military leadership and mustering the tribes

gifts.name: The Spirit came upon him; prophesied

events.title: Looking for donkeys, finds a kingdom
events.summary: Searching for his father's lost donkeys, the tall Benjaminite meets Samuel, whom God has told to expect Israel's leader.

events.title: Anointed and chosen by lot
events.summary: Samuel anoints him privately; signs follow and he prophesies. At Mizpah the lot falls on him while he hides among the baggage.

events.title: Rescues Jabesh-gilead
events.summary: Moved by the Spirit, he summons the tribes, defeats Nahash the Ammonite, spares his critics and is confirmed king at Gilgal.

events.title: Unlawful sacrifice at Gilgal
events.summary: With the Philistines massing and troops deserting, Saul offers the burnt offering before Samuel arrives. Samuel says his kingdom will not continue.

events.title: Rash oath during the Michmash battle
events.summary: Saul forbids food until evening; Jonathan unknowingly eats honey, and Saul is ready to execute him until the troops ransom him.

events.title: Spares Agag; rejected as king
events.summary: Commanded to devote Amalek to destruction, Saul keeps the king and the best livestock. Samuel announces God's rejection; tearing Samuel's robe becomes a sign of the torn kingdom.

events.title: Spirit departs; David plays the lyre
events.summary: An evil spirit from the LORD torments him, and young David is brought to soothe him with music.

events.title: Jealousy and pursuit of David
events.summary: After the women sing that David has slain his ten thousands, Saul twice hurls a spear at him and then hunts him through the wilderness.

events.title: Massacre of the priests of Nob
events.summary: Believing the priests aided David, Saul has Doeg the Edomite kill eighty-five priests and strike the town.

events.title: Spared by David at En-gedi
events.summary: David cuts off the corner of Saul's robe in a cave but refuses to harm the LORD's anointed; Saul weeps and admits David will be king.

events.title: Consults the medium at Endor
events.summary: Receiving no answer from God, Saul disguises himself and seeks a medium, who brings up Samuel. He hears that he will die the next day.

events.title: Death on Mount Gilboa
events.summary: With three sons killed and himself badly wounded by Philistine archers, Saul falls on his own sword. The men of Jabesh-gilead recover and bury the bodies.

journey.note: Home town and later royal seat ('Gibeah of Saul').
Meets Samuel while searching for donkeys (town unnamed in the text; traditionally Samuel's Ramah).
Publicly chosen by lot.
Kingship renewed; later his unlawful sacrifice and rejection.
Pursuing David; spared in the cave.
Final battle with the Philistines and death.

summary:
Saul son of Kish, a tall Benjaminite, was Israel's first king. Anointed by Samuel in answer to the people's demand for a king, he began with promise: the Spirit came on him, he rescued Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonites, and he fought the Philistines and other enemies on every side.

His reign then unravels through acts of impatient or partial obedience, above all offering sacrifice without Samuel and sparing Agag and Amalek's livestock. Samuel announces that God has rejected him. The rest of the story traces his decline into fear, jealousy of David, violent suspicion, and finally a desperate visit to a medium before he dies on Mount Gilboa.

Saul is one of Scripture's most tragic figures. The narrative is sympathetic to his torment while holding him responsible, and David's lament over him and Jonathan is among the most moving poems in the Bible.
textSays: Son of Kish of Benjamin, taller than anyone (1 Sam 9:2). Anointed by Samuel (1 Sam 10:1), confirmed after victory at Jabesh (1 Sam 11). Rejected for disobedience (1 Sam 13:13-14; 15:23). Tormented by an evil spirit from the LORD (1 Sam 16:14), pursued David, died at Gilboa (1 Sam 31). The length of his reign is textually damaged in 1 Sam 13:1; Acts 13:21 gives forty years. Chronicles says he died for unfaithfulness and for consulting a medium (1 Chr 10:13-14).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition is relatively gentle on Saul, noting his humility (hiding among the baggage) and the fact that he sinned fewer times than David; his downfall is attributed to misplaced mercy and failure to obey precisely. Some midrashim stress that he went to his death knowingly, accepting judgment.

Saul often serves as a type of the person who begins in grace but falls through pride and disobedience; Gregory the Great used him as an example for rulers. Debate continues on whether the figure at Endor was truly Samuel or a demonic deception.

Saul illustrates that external anointing and spiritual experience do not equal saving faith; his rejection shows God's sovereignty in choosing David. Some Reformed writers stress his culpability; others note God's providence in giving the people the king they asked for.

Many scholars think the narrative was shaped in David's court to legitimise David's dynasty, so Saul may have been a more effective ruler than portrayed. Others argue the text's own sympathy for Saul tells against crude propaganda.

strengths: Magnanimity toward critics after victory (1 Sam 11:13)
failures: Impatient sacrifice (1 Sam 13)
Partial obedience and blame-shifting regarding Amalek (1 Sam 15)
Murderous jealousy of David
Slaughter of the priests of Nob
Consulting a medium

context: Saul's kingdom was small and largely tribal, centred on Benjamin and the central hills, with no capital city, standing bureaucracy or temple. The Philistines held a monopoly on iron-working (1 Sam 13:19-22) and garrisons in the hill country. Tell el-Ful north of Jerusalem is commonly identified with Gibeah, though excavated remains there are debated.
legacy: His failure shapes the Bible's theology of kingship: a king must be subject to God's word through the prophet. His house survived briefly through Ish-bosheth, and his grandson Mephibosheth was cared for by David. The apostle Paul, also a Benjaminite named Saul, was named after him (Acts 13:21; Phil 3:5).
voice: Charismatic but insecure; swings between warmth and suspicion, defends himself with excuses, and in his last days speaks with haunted desperation.

gifts.name: Faith that God can save by many or by few

events.title: Attacks the Philistine garrison
events.summary: With only his armour-bearer he climbs to a Philistine outpost near Michmash, trusting God, and triggers a panic that becomes a general rout.

events.title: Breaks his father's oath unknowingly
events.summary: He eats honey not knowing Saul's ban; Saul would have him killed, but the army ransoms him.

events.title: Covenant with David
events.summary: After David kills Goliath, Jonathan loves him as himself and gives him his robe, armour, sword, bow and belt.

events.title: Warns and protects David
events.summary: He pleads with Saul for David and later uses the arrow signal in the field to tell David he must flee.

events.title: Strengthens David at Horesh
events.summary: He finds David in the wilderness of Ziph, encourages him in God and says David will be king with Jonathan second to him.

events.title: Killed at Gilboa
events.summary: He dies with his father and brothers; David laments him in the Song of the Bow.

summary: Jonathan, Saul's eldest son and heir, is one of the most admirable figures in Samuel: a brave warrior who trusted God against long odds and a friend who bound himself to David by covenant even though David's rise cost him the throne. He repeatedly protected David from Saul while remaining loyal to his father, and died beside him at Gilboa. David honoured their covenant by caring for Jonathan's son Mephibosheth (2 Sam 9).
textSays: Son of Saul; led a thousand men at Gibeah (1 Sam 13:2). Loved David as his own soul and made a covenant with him (1 Sam 18:1-3; 20:16-17). Died at Gilboa (1 Sam 31:2). David's lament says his love was more wonderful than the love of women (2 Sam 1:26).

interpretations.view: The Mishnah (Avot 5:16) holds up the love of David and Jonathan as the model of love that does not depend on any ulterior cause.
Their bond is read as covenant friendship and self-giving loyalty; Jonathan's yielding of his claim to David is compared to John the Baptist's 'he must increase'.

Some interpreters read the relationship as romantic or erotic, pointing to the language of 2 Sam 1:26 and 1 Sam 20:30-41. Others reply that 'love' (ahavah) is standard covenant and political-loyalty vocabulary in the ancient Near East, and that the lament's comparison does not imply a sexual relationship. The question is debated.

voice: Warm, frank and brave; speaks with quick conviction about God's power and with tender loyalty to his friend, while honouring his father.

events.title: Loves David and marries him
events.summary: Saul offers her to David for a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping David will die; David doubles it and marries her.

events.title: Helps David escape
events.summary: She lets David down through a window and puts a household idol in his bed to delay Saul's men.

events.title: Given to another man, then taken back
events.summary: Saul gives her to Paltiel; later David demands her return as a condition of a deal with Abner, and Paltiel follows weeping.

events.title: Despises David dancing before the ark
events.summary: She rebukes David for dancing uncovered before servant girls; he replies he danced before the LORD. The text notes she had no child to the day of her death.

summary: Michal, Saul's younger daughter, is the only woman in the Hebrew Bible said to love a man. She married David, saved his life from her father, was given to another husband in his absence, and was later reclaimed by David for political reasons. Her final scene, scorning David's dance before the ark, ends with the note that she had no child, closing off any heir uniting the houses of Saul and David.
textSays: Daughter of Saul who loved David (1 Sam 18:20). She saved him (1 Sam 19:11-17), was given to Paltiel (1 Sam 25:44), was returned to David (2 Sam 3:13-16), despised him at the ark's arrival and had no child (2 Sam 6:16-23). 2 Sam 21:8 in the Hebrew and KJV names Michal as mother of five sons, but most manuscripts of the Septuagint and many translations read Merab (cf. 1 Sam 18:19).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic sources sometimes resolve 2 Sam 21:8 by saying Michal raised Merab's sons. Some midrashim present her positively, as pious and wise.
She is often read as a warning against contempt for wholehearted worship.

Many modern readers see her as a woman used as a political pawn by both Saul and David, whose bitterness is understandable. Others reply that the narrator still presents her scorn as misjudging David's worship; both elements may be intended.

voice: Proud and sharp-tongued, with the bearing of a king's daughter; once passionate, later bitter.

skills.name: Sling and close combat; military command

gifts.name: The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him from his anointing

events.title: Anointed by Samuel
events.summary: The youngest son of Jesse, out keeping sheep, is anointed in front of his brothers; the Spirit comes on him from that day.

events.title: Defeats Goliath
events.summary: In the Valley of Elah he faces the Philistine champion with a sling, declaring that the battle is the LORD's, and kills him.

events.title: At Saul's court; friendship with Jonathan
events.summary: His success makes him popular and Saul jealous; Jonathan covenants with him and Michal marries him.

events.title: Fugitive years
events.summary: Fleeing Saul, he feigns madness at Gath, gathers four hundred distressed men at the cave of Adullam and moves through the wilderness of Judah.

events.title: Spares Saul twice
events.summary: Twice he has Saul at his mercy and refuses to strike the LORD's anointed.

events.title: Vassal of Achish at Ziklag
events.summary: He serves the Philistine king Achish from Ziklag while raiding Israel's enemies, and recovers his people after an Amalekite raid.

events.title: King at Hebron, then over all Israel
events.summary: Judah anoints him at Hebron; after civil war with Saul's house he is anointed king over all Israel, reigning forty years in total.

events.title: Captures Jerusalem and brings up the ark
events.summary: He takes the Jebusite stronghold, makes it the City of David, and brings the ark there amid dancing and sacrifice.

events.title: The Davidic covenant
events.summary: Wanting to build God a house, he is told instead that God will build him a house: a dynasty and throne established forever.

events.title: Adultery with Bathsheba and murder of Uriah
events.summary: He takes Bathsheba, and when she is pregnant arranges her husband Uriah's death in battle.

events.title: Confronted by Nathan; repents
events.summary: Nathan's parable of the poor man's lamb exposes him. He confesses; he is forgiven but told the sword will not depart from his house.

events.title: Absalom's rebellion
events.summary: Driven from Jerusalem, he climbs the Mount of Olives weeping. After Absalom's death he mourns, 'O my son Absalom'.

events.title: Census and plague; buys the threshing floor
events.summary: His census brings a plague; he buys Araunah's threshing floor and builds an altar there, later the temple site (2 Chr 3:1).

events.title: Makes Solomon king and dies
events.summary: Prompted by Nathan and Bathsheba, he has Solomon anointed, charges him to keep God's law, and dies after reigning forty years.

Serves at Saul's court.
First flight: to Samuel at Naioth.
Feigns madness before Achish.
Cave of Adullam; his band forms.
Leaves his parents with the king of Moab at Mizpeh of Moab.
Strongholds of En-gedi; spares Saul in the cave.
Returns to Achish as a vassal.
Base for sixteen months.
Anointed king of Judah, later of all Israel.
Captures the city and makes it his capital.
Flight from Absalom.
Crosses the Jordan to Mahanaim; later returns.

summary:
David son of Jesse is the central king of the Old Testament: a shepherd boy anointed by Samuel, the giant-killer of the Valley of Elah, a fugitive from Saul who refused to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, and finally the king who united the tribes, captured Jerusalem and made it the political and religious capital of Israel.

God's covenant with him in 2 Samuel 7, promising a house and a throne forever, becomes the foundation of Israel's messianic hope. Prophets look for a coming son of David, and the New Testament opens by calling Jesus the son of David. Many psalms are linked to him by their headings, and he is remembered as Israel's model worshipper.

The text does not idealise him. His adultery with Bathsheba and murder of Uriah are told in plain detail, and the second half of his reign is shadowed by violence within his own family: Amnon's rape of Tamar, Absalom's revolt and death, and the struggle over succession. His greatness in the narrative lies less in moral perfection than in his repentance and his trust in God's mercy.
textSays: Youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem (1 Sam 16:10-13). Anointed by Samuel; killed Goliath (1 Sam 17); fled Saul; anointed king at Hebron, ruling seven and a half years there and thirty-three in Jerusalem (2 Sam 5:4-5). Received God's covenant of an everlasting dynasty (2 Sam 7:12-16). Committed adultery and murder, was rebuked by Nathan and repented (2 Sam 11-12). Called a man after God's own heart (1 Sam 13:14; Acts 13:22). Seventy-three psalms carry 'of David' in their Hebrew headings.

interpretations.view: David is the ideal king and ancestor of the Messiah (Mashiach ben David). Rabbinic tradition credits him with composing or compiling the book of Psalms and treats his repentance as a model of teshuvah. The Talmud debates the extent of his sin with Bathsheba, some sages arguing soldiers' wives were conditionally divorced, a view others reject.

David is honoured as prophet and saint and as a type of Christ, the shepherd-king born in Bethlehem. Psalm 51 became the church's classic penitential psalm, and the Psalter attributed to him is the backbone of the daily office.

The Davidic covenant is a key stage in covenant theology, fulfilled in Christ, the son of David who reigns forever (Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:29-36). David's sin and forgiveness illustrate justification apart from works (Rom 4:6-8).

The Tel Dan inscription (9th century BC) is widely read as mentioning the 'House of David', supporting a historical founder. Scholars debate the size of his kingdom: maximalists accept a substantial state; minimalists and some archaeologists (low chronology) see a modest chiefdom later idealised. Many also read the Succession Narrative (2 Sam 9-20; 1 Kgs 1-2) as either court apologetic or unusually candid royal history.

strengths: Refusal to seize the throne by violence against Saul (1 Sam 24:6)
failures: Adultery with Bathsheba and murder of Uriah (2 Sam 11)
Passivity after Amnon raped Tamar (2 Sam 13:21)
Indulgence of Absalom
The census (2 Sam 24:10)
Deathbed instructions for revenge on Joab and Shimei (1 Kgs 2:5-9)

context: David rose in the gap left by declining Egyptian and Hittite power, before Assyria's expansion, when small states could form in the Levant. Philistine pressure, the Saulide-Judahite rivalry and the neutral Jebusite city of Jerusalem explain many of his political moves. Excavations in the City of David (e.g. the Stepped Stone Structure) and at Khirbet Qeiyafa are cited in debates about 10th-century Judah.
legacy: Founder of the dynasty that ruled Judah for about four centuries, organiser of Israel's worship (1 Chr 15-16; 23-26), and the figure through whom messianic hope is expressed: Isa 11:1, Jer 23:5, Ezek 34:23-24. Jesus is called son of David (Matt 1:1) and the root and offspring of David (Rev 22:16).

traditions.text: David was the author or editor of the whole book of Psalms, compiling also psalms by ten elders.
A building on Mount Zion has been venerated as David's tomb since the medieval period; most archaeologists consider it unlikely to be authentic, since 1 Kgs 2:10 places the tomb in the City of David.
Islam honours David (Dawud) as a prophet to whom the Zabur (Psalms) was given.

voice: Passionate and poetic; moves quickly from boldness to tears, speaks to God as to a close friend, and turns crises into songs.

roles: wife of Nabal, then of David

events.title: Intercepts David's revenge
events.summary: When her husband Nabal insults David's men, she brings provisions, meets David on the road and talks him out of bloodshed.

events.title: Widowed and marries David
events.summary: Nabal dies ten days after hearing what she did; David sends for her and she becomes his wife.

events.title: Captured and rescued at Ziklag
events.summary: Amalekites carry her off in a raid; David recovers her and the others.

events.title: Mother of David's second son
events.summary: At Hebron she bears Chileab, also called Daniel.

summary: Abigail, wife of the wealthy and boorish Nabal of Carmel in Judah, is described as intelligent and beautiful. Her quick action and wise speech kept David from avenging himself on Nabal, and her words anticipated God's 'sure house' for David. After Nabal's death she became David's wife, shared his outlaw years at Ziklag, and bore him a son at Hebron.
textSays: A woman of good understanding and beautiful (1 Sam 25:3). She persuaded David not to shed blood (1 Sam 25:32-33), married him (1 Sam 25:42), and bore Chileab/Daniel (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:1).

interpretations.view: The Talmud (Megillah 14a-b) counts Abigail among the seven women prophets because of her prediction about David.
Often presented as an example of wise peacemaking and courage in a household ruled by a foolish man.

voice: Calm, gracious and persuasive; uses careful courtesy and theological argument to turn an angry man aside.

names.meaning: Daughter of an oath, or daughter of seven

events.title: Taken by David
events.summary: Seen bathing from the palace roof, she is sent for by David while her husband is at war, and becomes pregnant.

events.title: Widowed and married to David; the child dies
events.summary: After Uriah is killed she mourns and David marries her; the child dies as Nathan foretold.

events.title: Birth of Solomon
events.summary: David comforts her and she bears Solomon, whom the LORD loves.

events.title: Secures Solomon's succession
events.summary: With Nathan she reminds the aged David of his oath, and he orders Solomon's anointing.

events.title: Queen mother
events.summary: Solomon seats her at his right hand; she carries Adonijah's request for Abishag, which Solomon treats as treason.

summary: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite, enters the story as the object of David's adultery and becomes the mother of Solomon. Later she is a decisive political actor, working with Nathan to secure Solomon's succession, and serves as queen mother. Matthew names her, as 'the wife of Uriah', in Jesus' genealogy.
textSays: Daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah (2 Sam 11:3). David sent for her and lay with her (2 Sam 11:4). She bore Solomon (2 Sam 12:24) and three other sons (1 Chr 3:5). She acted with Nathan for Solomon (1 Kgs 1:15-31). Listed in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:6).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition tends to exonerate her and sometimes identifies her as the mother who taught Lemuel (Prov 31:1), with Lemuel understood as Solomon.
Older commentary sometimes faulted her for bathing in view of the palace; this is now widely rejected, since the text places all blame on David (2 Sam 11:27; 12:9).

Debate centres on her agency: many read 2 Sam 11 as an abuse of royal power amounting to coercion, while others see her later actions in 1 Kgs 1 as showing a shrewd political figure. These are not mutually exclusive.

voice: Measured and dignified; in her later years speaks with the careful, formal courtesy of a seasoned court figure.

events.title: Refuses to go home
events.summary: Recalled by David to cover up the pregnancy, he refuses to sleep with his wife while the ark and army are in the field.

events.title: Killed at Rabbah by David's order
events.summary: He carries his own death warrant to Joab and is placed where the fighting is fiercest.

summary: Uriah the Hittite, one of David's thirty mighty men, was Bathsheba's husband. His integrity, refusing comfort while his comrades were at war, sharply contrasts with David's conduct, and David had him killed at the siege of Rabbah. His name stands in the genealogy of Jesus as 'the wife of Uriah'.
textSays: A Hittite among David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:39), husband of Bathsheba, killed on David's orders (2 Sam 11; 12:9).
voice: Plain-spoken soldier with an unbending sense of duty and loyalty.

events.title: Delivers the Davidic covenant
events.summary: He first approves David's plan to build a temple, then returns with God's word: David's son will build it, and God will establish David's house forever.

events.title: Confronts David: 'You are the man'
events.summary: Through the parable of the poor man's ewe lamb he leads David to condemn himself, then pronounces judgment and forgiveness.

events.title: Names Solomon Jedidiah
events.summary: God sends him to call the child Jedidiah, 'beloved of the LORD'.

events.title: Secures Solomon's accession
events.summary: When Adonijah claims the throne, he coordinates with Bathsheba and anoints Solomon with Zadok.

summary: Nathan was the prophet at David's court who both announced God's everlasting covenant with David's house and confronted the king over Bathsheba and Uriah with the parable of the ewe lamb. In David's old age he engineered Solomon's succession. Chronicles credits him with histories of David and Solomon and with helping organise temple music.
textSays: Prophet who delivered the covenant oracle (2 Sam 7), rebuked David (2 Sam 12), named Solomon Jedidiah (2 Sam 12:25), backed Solomon's anointing (1 Kgs 1), wrote records (1 Chr 29:29; 2 Chr 9:29), and gave commands on Levitical music (2 Chr 29:25).

interpretations.view: Nathan is the model of the prophet who speaks truth to power with courage and skill; his 'You are the man' is a classic of moral confrontation.
Some read 1 Kgs 1 as showing Nathan as a partisan court politician as much as a prophet; others see no conflict between prophetic office and political engagement.

voice: Tactful, wise and fearless; tells stories to make hard truths land, then speaks bluntly.

events.title: Tells David to leave the stronghold
events.summary: He directs the fugitive David to go into the land of Judah.

events.title: Offers David three punishments after the census
events.summary: He brings God's choice of famine, flight or plague, then tells David to build an altar on Araunah's threshing floor.

summary: Gad was a prophet who accompanied David from his fugitive days, guiding his movements and later announcing judgment for the census and the site of the altar that became the temple mount. Chronicles credits him with a record of David's reign and with arranging temple music alongside Nathan.
textSays: Prophet with David in the stronghold (1 Sam 22:5), David's seer at the census (2 Sam 24:11), author of records (1 Chr 29:29), involved in Levitical music (2 Chr 29:25).
voice: Brief and direct; delivers God's word without embellishment.

events.title: Murders Abner
events.summary: He kills Saul's general Abner in revenge for his brother Asahel, undermining David's peace with the north.

events.title: Leads the capture of Jerusalem
events.summary: He goes up first against the Jebusites and becomes chief commander.

events.title: Arranges Uriah's death
events.summary: He carries out David's order to have Uriah killed at Rabbah.

events.title: Kills Absalom
events.summary: Against David's order he kills Absalom hanging in a tree, then rebukes David for mourning instead of thanking his troops.

events.title: Executed at the altar
events.summary: Having backed Adonijah, he flees to the altar; Solomon has Benaiah kill him there.

summary: Joab, son of David's sister Zeruiah, commanded David's army for most of his reign. Loyal to David's throne and ruthlessly effective, he also murdered rivals (Abner, Amasa), carried out David's plot against Uriah, and killed Absalom against orders. He backed Adonijah in the succession struggle and was executed at Solomon's command.
textSays: Son of Zeruiah (2 Sam 2:18), commander of the army (2 Sam 8:16). Killed Abner (2 Sam 3:27), Absalom (2 Sam 18:14) and Amasa (2 Sam 20:10). Supported Adonijah (1 Kgs 1:7) and was killed by Benaiah (1 Kgs 2:34).

interpretations.view: Joab is read as the archetype of the loyal but unscrupulous servant whose pragmatism serves the king while violating justice. David's 'these sons of Zeruiah are too hard for me' (2 Sam 3:39) captures the tension.

voice: Blunt, hard-headed and impatient with sentiment; speaks like a soldier who believes results justify means.

events.title: Avenges Tamar by killing Amnon
events.summary: After Amnon rapes his sister Tamar and David does nothing, Absalom waits two years and has Amnon killed, then flees to Geshur.

events.title: Returns through Joab's scheme
events.summary: Joab uses a wise woman of Tekoa to persuade David to bring him back; father and son are reconciled after two more years.

events.title: Steals the hearts of Israel
events.summary: He stands at the city gate promising justice to all who come with complaints.

events.title: Proclaimed king at Hebron
events.summary: He launches his revolt at Hebron, David flees, and he takes Jerusalem and his father's concubines.

events.title: Dies in the forest of Ephraim
events.summary: Caught by his head in an oak, he is killed by Joab. David grieves bitterly.

summary: Absalom, David's handsome third son by Maacah of Geshur, killed his half-brother Amnon to avenge his sister Tamar, then won popular support and led a full-scale revolt that drove David from Jerusalem. His defeat and death in the forest of Ephraim produced David's famous lament. His story fulfils Nathan's word that the sword would not depart from David's house.
textSays: Son of David and Maacah (2 Sam 3:3), famous for his beauty and hair (2 Sam 14:25-26). Killed Amnon (2 Sam 13:28-29), rebelled (2 Sam 15), slept with David's concubines (2 Sam 16:22, cf. 2 Sam 12:11), was killed by Joab (2 Sam 18:14). Psalm 3 is headed as written when David fled from him.

interpretations.view: The Mishnah (Sotah 1:8) notes that he took pride in his hair and was caught by it, an example of measure for measure.
Often read as a study in ambition and in the consequences of David's failures as a father; David's lament is cited as an image of parental and divine grief.

voice: Smooth, flattering and aggrieved; presents himself as the champion of the overlooked while nursing resentment.

gifts.name: Wisdom and understanding given by God

events.title: Birth and naming
events.summary: Born to David and Bathsheba after the death of their first child; the LORD loves him and Nathan names him Jedidiah.

events.title: Anointed king at Gihon
events.summary: When Adonijah claims the throne, David orders Solomon anointed by Zadok and Nathan at the Gihon spring.

events.title: Consolidates power
events.summary: He has Adonijah, Joab and Shimei executed and banishes Abiathar; 'the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon'.

events.title: Asks for wisdom at Gibeon
events.summary: In a dream God offers him anything; he asks for an understanding heart to govern, and is promised riches and honour too.

events.title: Judgment between two mothers
events.summary: He orders a disputed baby cut in two and identifies the true mother by her compassion.

events.title: Builds the temple
events.summary: With Hiram of Tyre's cedar and craftsmen he builds the temple over seven years, beginning in his fourth year, 480 years after the exodus by 1 Kgs 6:1.

events.title: Dedicates the temple
events.summary: The ark is brought in, the glory cloud fills the house, and Solomon prays that God will hear prayers made toward this place, even from foreigners and exiles.

events.title: Fortifies Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer
events.summary: He uses forced labour to build the Millo, the wall of Jerusalem and royal cities.

events.title: Visit of the queen of Sheba
events.summary: She tests him with hard questions and declares that his wisdom and prosperity exceed the report.

events.title: Foreign wives and idolatry
events.summary: His seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines turn his heart to other gods in his old age; God announces the kingdom will be torn from his son.

events.title: Adversaries arise; death
events.summary: Hadad, Rezon and Jeroboam oppose him. He dies after forty years and Rehoboam succeeds.

summary:
Solomon, son of David and Bathsheba, ruled Israel at the height of its power and wealth. Asking God for wisdom rather than riches, he became proverbial for it, and he built the temple in Jerusalem that became the centre of Israel's worship for nearly four hundred years. His prayer at its dedication is one of the great prayers of the Old Testament.

His reign also had a darker side that the text does not hide. He secured the throne through executions, laid heavy forced labour and taxation on the northern tribes, multiplied horses, silver and wives against the warnings of Deut 17:16-17, and in old age built shrines for the gods of his foreign wives. God's verdict is that the kingdom will be divided after him, which happens at once under his son Rehoboam.

Tradition links Solomon with Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, and Jesus refers to his glory and his wisdom as benchmarks that the kingdom of God surpasses.
textSays: Son of David and Bathsheba (2 Sam 12:24), anointed king (1 Kgs 1:39), asked for wisdom (1 Kgs 3:9), built the temple and palace (1 Kgs 6-7), wrote 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs (1 Kgs 4:32), loved many foreign women who turned his heart (1 Kgs 11:1-4), reigned forty years (1 Kgs 11:42). Headings attribute parts of Proverbs (Prov 1:1; 10:1; 25:1), the Song (Song 1:1) and Pss 72 and 127 to him; Ecclesiastes speaks as 'son of David, king in Jerusalem' (Eccl 1:1). Jesus says one greater than Solomon is here (Matt 12:42).

interpretations.view: Solomon is the wise king and temple builder; rabbinic tradition attributes the Song, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes to him at different stages of life, while critiquing his marriages. Later legends make him master of demons and speaker with animals.

Solomon is read as a type of Christ the wise king and temple builder; the Wisdom of Solomon (deuterocanonical) is associated with his name. Patristic writers disputed whether he finally repented, some reading Ecclesiastes as a confession of old age.

Emphasis falls on the danger of a divided heart: a king blessed with wisdom who failed to obey. Many evangelicals hold Solomonic authorship of most of Proverbs and of Ecclesiastes and Song; others accept that Ecclesiastes uses a Solomonic persona.

Scholars debate the scale of Solomon's kingdom. Some attribute the six-chambered gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer to Solomon (Yadin, Mazar); the low chronology (Finkelstein) dates them to the 9th-century Omrides. No contemporary inscription names Solomon. Most critical scholars date Ecclesiastes to the Persian or Hellenistic period.

strengths: Temple building and dedicatory prayer (1 Kgs 8)
failures: Heavy forced labour (1 Kgs 5:13-14; 12:4)
Accumulating horses, gold and wives (1 Kgs 10:26-11:3; Deut 17:16-17)
Building shrines to Chemosh and Molech (1 Kgs 11:7-8)
turningPoints: Temple dedication and second appearance of God (1 Kgs 9:1-9)

context: Solomon's reign falls in a period of weak Egyptian and Mesopotamian power, letting a Levantine kingdom control trade routes. He allied with Hiram of Tyre and married Pharaoh's daughter (1 Kgs 3:1), notable since Egyptian princesses were rarely given to foreign kings. The temple's plan (porch, hall, inner sanctuary) has close parallels in Syrian temples such as Ain Dara and Tell Tayinat.
legacy: The temple shaped Israelite worship until 586 BC, and Solomon's prayer framed later Jewish prayer toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10). His failures are blamed for the split of the kingdom (1 Kgs 11:11-13). Wisdom literature was gathered under his name, and later Jewish, Christian and Islamic tradition (Sulayman) made him the archetype of the wise king.

traditions.text: Solomon wrote the Song of Songs in youth, Proverbs in maturity and Ecclesiastes in old age.
traditions.source: Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1 (section number needs verification)

traditions.text: Hezekiah and his colleagues wrote down (edited) Proverbs, the Song and Ecclesiastes.
Solomon commanded demons through a ring given by God, used to build the temple.
traditions.source: Testament of Solomon (pseudepigraphal, early centuries AD)

traditions.text: The Ethiopian royal line descends from Menelik I, son of Solomon and the queen of Sheba.

voice: Eloquent and measured, fond of balanced sayings and observations about nature and human folly; in later life weary and reflective.

events.title: Visits Solomon
events.summary: Hearing of Solomon's fame, she comes with a great caravan of spices, gold and stones, tests him with hard questions, and blesses the LORD for setting him on the throne.

journey.note: Her kingdom, usually located in south-west Arabia (Yemen).
Visits Solomon's court.
Returns to her own land.

summary: An unnamed queen of Sheba, a kingdom usually located in south-west Arabia, travelled to Jerusalem to test Solomon's wisdom and exchange rich gifts, possibly also on trade business. Jesus cites her as a Gentile who came from the ends of the earth to hear wisdom and will condemn his unbelieving generation. Ethiopian and Islamic traditions developed extensive stories about her.
textSays: Came to test Solomon with hard questions, was overwhelmed by his wisdom and court, praised the LORD, exchanged gifts and returned home (1 Kgs 10:1-13). Jesus calls her the queen of the south (Matt 12:42; Luke 11:31).

interpretations.view: Identified as Makeda, whose son by Solomon, Menelik I, founded the Solomonic dynasty and brought the ark to Aksum (Kebra Nagast).

Sabaean inscriptions confirm a powerful incense-trading kingdom in Yemen, though its monarchy is attested mainly from the 8th century BC; some locate Sheba in north Arabia or link it with Ethiopia. No extra-biblical source names this queen.

traditions.text: Her son Menelik I by Solomon founded Ethiopia's royal line.
The Qur'an tells of a queen of Saba who comes to Solomon and submits to God; later commentators name her Bilqis.

voice: Regal, curious and testing; asks searching questions and is generous with praise once convinced.

events.title: Rejects the elders' counsel at Shechem
events.summary: Asked to lighten Solomon's yoke, he follows his young advisers and promises scorpions instead of whips.

events.title: The northern tribes secede
events.summary: Israel cries 'To your tents', stones his labour chief Adoram, and makes Jeroboam king.

events.title: Forbidden to fight the north
events.summary: The prophet Shemaiah stops his campaign to reconquer Israel.

events.title: Shishak plunders Jerusalem
events.summary: In his fifth year Pharaoh Shishak takes the temple and palace treasures; Rehoboam replaces gold shields with bronze.

summary: Rehoboam, Solomon's son by Naamah the Ammonite, inherited a kingdom already strained by heavy labour and taxes. His harsh answer at Shechem triggered the secession of the ten northern tribes under Jeroboam, leaving him with Judah and Benjamin. His reign also saw religious decline and the invasion of Pharaoh Shishak, an event confirmed by Sheshonq I's relief at Karnak.
textSays: Son of Solomon and Naamah the Ammonite; reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 14:21). His harsh reply split the kingdom (1 Kgs 12:13-16). Judah built high places and pillars under him (1 Kgs 14:22-24). Chronicles adds his fortifications, his humbling before Shishak, and eighteen wives (2 Chr 11-12). Listed in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:7).

interpretations.view: The Shechem episode is a classic lesson in servant leadership: the elders advise that if he serves the people they will serve him forever (1 Kgs 12:7). The text also sees God's hand fulfilling Ahijah's word (1 Kgs 12:15).
The Karnak list of Sheshonq I names many towns in Israel and the Negev but, as preserved, not Jerusalem, prompting debate over whether Jerusalem paid tribute rather than being attacked.

voice: Brash and status-conscious, eager to prove himself tougher than his father; later chastened.

names.meaning: The people contends, or may the people multiply

roles: first king of the northern kingdom

events.title: Promised ten tribes by Ahijah
events.summary: The prophet Ahijah tears his cloak into twelve pieces and gives him ten; God promises him a lasting house if he obeys. Solomon seeks to kill him and he flees to Shishak in Egypt.

events.title: Made king of Israel
events.summary: Returning after Solomon's death, he is made king by the northern tribes and fortifies Shechem.

events.title: Golden calves at Bethel and Dan
events.summary: Fearing pilgrimages to Jerusalem, he sets up two calves, appoints non-Levitical priests and a new feast in the eighth month.

events.title: Rebuked by the man of God from Judah
events.summary: A prophet foretells Josiah's desecration of the altar; Jeroboam's outstretched hand withers and is restored.

events.title: Ahijah foretells his house's end
events.summary: His disguised wife consults the blind Ahijah about their sick son, who dies as she enters Tirzah.

summary: Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite official under Solomon, was promised the northern tribes by the prophet Ahijah, fled to Egypt, and became the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after Rehoboam's folly. To keep his people from worshipping in Jerusalem, he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Kings measures nearly every later northern ruler by whether he walked in 'the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat'.
textSays: An Ephraimite placed over the forced labour of Joseph (1 Kgs 11:26-28). Ahijah gave him ten tribes on condition of obedience (1 Kgs 11:38). He made two golden calves, saying 'Behold your gods, O Israel' (1 Kgs 12:28). Reigned twenty-two years (1 Kgs 14:20).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition counts him among those who caused the many to sin; the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 10:2) lists him among kings with no share in the world to come.

Many scholars suggest the calves were meant as pedestals for an invisible YHWH (like the cherubim) rather than idols, and that the Deuteronomistic writers judged the northern cult from a Jerusalem perspective. Others note that the text itself treats this distinction as irrelevant because the cult broke covenant law.

voice: Shrewd and capable, driven by political insecurity; justifies religious innovation as practical necessity.

events.title: Marries Jezebel and serves Baal
events.summary: He marries the Sidonian princess and builds a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria.

events.title: Drought and contest on Carmel
events.summary: After three years of drought he meets Elijah ('troubler of Israel'), witnesses fire from heaven on Carmel, and rides to Jezreel ahead of the rain.

events.title: Victories over Ben-hadad
events.summary: Encouraged by prophets he defeats the Arameans twice, but spares Ben-hadad and is condemned for it.

events.title: Naboth's vineyard
events.summary: Jezebel has Naboth judicially murdered so Ahab can take his vineyard; Elijah pronounces doom, and Ahab's repentance delays it.

events.title: Death at Ramoth-gilead
events.summary: Ignoring Micaiah's warning he goes to battle in disguise, is struck by a random arrow and dies; dogs lick his blood in Samaria.

summary: Ahab son of Omri ruled the northern kingdom for twenty-two years and was, by Assyrian evidence, one of the strongest kings of his day. Kings judges him the most wicked Israelite king for promoting Baal worship with his wife Jezebel. His reign is the setting of Elijah's ministry, the contest on Mount Carmel and the murder of Naboth. He died in battle at Ramoth-gilead, as Micaiah had foretold.
textSays: Son of Omri; did more evil than all before him (1 Kgs 16:30). Married Jezebel and served Baal (1 Kgs 16:31-32). Humbled himself after Elijah's rebuke (1 Kgs 21:27-29). Killed at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 22:34-37).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic sources portray him as both very wicked and, in some respects, generous and honouring the Torah scholars; the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 10:2) excludes him from the world to come.

The Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III lists 'Ahab the Israelite' contributing 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers to the coalition at Qarqar in 853 BC. Scholars note the gap between his political strength and the biblical focus on his religious failure.

voice: Sulky, self-pitying and easily led, yet capable of bravado in war and of momentary contrition.

events.title: Kills the prophets of the LORD
events.summary: She persecutes the LORD's prophets while supporting 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah at her table.

events.title: Threatens Elijah
events.summary: After Carmel she vows to kill Elijah within a day, and he flees.

events.title: Engineers Naboth's death
events.summary: Using letters in Ahab's name she arranges false witnesses and Naboth's stoning, so Ahab can take his vineyard.

events.title: Death at Jezreel
events.summary: Painting her eyes and taunting Jehu from a window, she is thrown down by eunuchs and eaten by dogs, as Elijah foretold.

summary: Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal king of Sidon, married Ahab and became the driving force behind Baal worship in Israel. She persecuted the LORD's prophets, threatened Elijah, and orchestrated the judicial murder of Naboth. She remained powerful as queen mother until Jehu's coup, when she was thrown from a window at Jezreel. In Revelation her name is applied to a false prophetess at Thyatira.
textSays: Daughter of Ethbaal of the Sidonians (1 Kgs 16:31). Killed prophets of the LORD (1 Kgs 18:4), threatened Elijah (1 Kgs 19:2), plotted Naboth's death (1 Kgs 21). Incited Ahab to evil (1 Kgs 21:25). Died as Elijah foretold (2 Kgs 9:36). Name used for a teacher at Thyatira (Rev 2:20).

interpretations.view: Jezebel is the archetype of the idolatrous, manipulative ruler; her name became a byword.

Some argue she acted as a loyal devotee of her own ancestral religion and as a capable queen in the Phoenician model of royal power, and that the sexualised later use of her name goes beyond the text. Others respond that the narrative's charge is not her gender but her violence and idolatry, which the text documents.
A seal inscribed 'yzbl' (Jezebel) of unknown provenance has been proposed as hers; the identification is debated.

voice: Imperious, sardonic and fearless; mocks weakness and speaks with the confidence of absolute royal power.

alternatives.label: If his letter to Jehoram (2 Chr 21:12) was written in his lifetime

gifts.name: Prayer that shut and opened the heavens
Miracles: provision and raising the dead

events.title: Announces drought
events.summary: He appears before Ahab declaring there will be neither dew nor rain except at his word.

events.title: Fed by ravens at the brook Cherith
events.summary: He hides east of the Jordan, drinking from the brook and fed by ravens until it dries up.

events.title: The widow of Zarephath
events.summary: In Phoenician territory a widow's flour and oil do not run out, and he raises her son from the dead.

events.title: Contest on Mount Carmel
events.summary: He challenges the people to stop limping between two opinions; Baal's prophets get no answer, and fire from the LORD consumes his drenched sacrifice. The prophets of Baal are killed at the Kishon.

events.title: Rain returns
events.summary: He prays seven times until a small cloud appears, then runs ahead of Ahab's chariot to Jezreel.

events.title: Flight to Horeb
events.summary: Threatened by Jezebel he flees past Beersheba, asks to die, is fed by an angel and travels forty days to Horeb, where God speaks not in wind, earthquake or fire but in a low whisper.

events.title: Calls Elisha
events.summary: He throws his cloak over Elisha, who is ploughing, and Elisha follows him.

events.title: Condemns Ahab over Naboth
events.summary: He meets Ahab in Naboth's vineyard and pronounces judgment on Ahab's house and Jezebel.

events.title: Confronts Ahaziah
events.summary: He intercepts messengers sent to consult Baal-zebub of Ekron, calls down fire on two companies of soldiers, and foretells the king's death.

events.title: Taken up in a whirlwind
events.summary: Travelling from Gilgal through Bethel and Jericho, he parts the Jordan with his cloak and is taken to heaven by a whirlwind as chariots of fire separate him from Elisha.

events.title: Promised return
events.summary: Malachi foretells that God will send Elijah before the great and dreadful day of the LORD.

events.title: At the transfiguration
events.summary: He appears with Moses talking with Jesus; Jesus says Elijah has already come, referring to John the Baptist.

journey.note: Home in Gilead (location uncertain).
Announces the drought to Ahab.
Brook Cherith, east of the Jordan.
Lodges with the widow in Sidonian territory.
Contest with the prophets of Baal.
Runs ahead of Ahab's chariot.
Leaves his servant and goes a day into the wilderness.
Forty days' journey; the still small voice.
Calls Elisha from the plough.
Confronts Ahab in Naboth's vineyard.
Final journey begins.
Visits the sons of the prophets.
Visits the sons of the prophets.
Parts the river and is taken up.

summary:
Elijah the Tishbite bursts into the story unannounced to confront Ahab and Jezebel's promotion of Baal, the storm and fertility god, with a drought that only the LORD can end. His ministry is one long argument that the LORD alone is God, climaxing on Mount Carmel when fire falls on his sacrifice after Baal's prophets have cried out all day in vain.

The story also shows his human frailty. Immediately after Carmel he flees from Jezebel's threat, asks to die, and is gently restored by God at Horeb, the mountain of Moses, where God speaks in a low whisper and gives him new work: anointing kings and a successor, Elisha. He is one of two people in the Old Testament who do not die but are taken by God, carried up in a whirlwind.

Malachi's promise that Elijah would return before the day of the LORD made him a figure of expectation. The Gospels identify John the Baptist as the Elijah who was to come, and Elijah himself appears with Moses at the transfiguration of Jesus.
textSays: A Tishbite from Gilead (1 Kgs 17:1), hairy and wearing a leather belt (2 Kgs 1:8). Announced drought, was fed by ravens and a widow, raised her son, defeated Baal's prophets on Carmel, fled to Horeb, called Elisha, condemned Ahab and Ahaziah, and was taken up by a whirlwind (2 Kgs 2:11). 2 Chr 21:12-15 records a letter from him to Jehoram of Judah. Malachi promises his return (Mal 4:5); Jesus identifies John the Baptist with that role (Matt 11:14; 17:12). James calls him a man with a nature like ours (Jas 5:17).

interpretations.view: Elijah is the herald of the Messiah. A cup is poured for him at the Passover Seder and a chair set for him at circumcisions; he is expected to resolve unanswered legal questions. Rabbinic stories show him appearing to sages and the poor.
Honoured as a saint (20 July). The Carmelite order looks to him as spiritual founder. Many fathers taught that Elijah and Enoch are the two witnesses of Rev 11 who will return before the end.

Most Protestants hold that Malachi's prophecy was fulfilled in John the Baptist, who came 'in the spirit and power of Elijah' (Luke 1:17); some dispensationalists expect a future literal return as one of the two witnesses.

The Elijah cycle is usually seen as prophetic legends from northern circles, incorporated into Kings, with the Carmel story as polemic against Baal's claim to control rain and fire. Scholars debate the Chronicler's letter to Jehoram, since 2 Kgs 3:11 suggests Elijah had already gone.

strengths: Single-minded zeal for the LORD (1 Kgs 19:10)
failures: Despair and wish to die after Carmel (1 Kgs 19:4)
Believing he alone was left faithful when seven thousand remained (1 Kgs 19:18)

context: Under the Omride dynasty, Israel had close ties with Phoenicia through Ahab's marriage to Jezebel. Baal Hadad was the Canaanite storm god believed to bring rain; a drought and fire from heaven struck at his claimed domain. Ugaritic texts describe Baal as 'rider of the clouds', which illuminates the contest.
legacy: Elijah became the model prophet: a lone voice against a corrupt establishment. His expected return shapes Jewish ritual and the Gospels' framing of John the Baptist and Jesus. Jesus cites his mission to a Gentile widow (Luke 4:25-26), and the disciples ask to call down fire like him (Luke 9:54).

traditions.text: Elijah is identified with Phinehas the zealous priest.
traditions.source: Pseudo-Philo, Biblical Antiquities 48.1; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Exod 6:18 (locators need verification)

traditions.text: A cup for Elijah is set at the Passover Seder and a chair of Elijah at circumcision ceremonies.
traditions.source: Medieval Jewish custom (Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer 29 for the chair; locator needs verification)

traditions.text: The Carmelite order traces its spiritual lineage to Elijah's presence on Mount Carmel.
traditions.source: Carmelite Rule of St Albert (c. 1209) and later Carmelite tradition

voice: Fiery, terse and dramatic; speaks in short, challenging sentences and sarcasm toward idols, but in private can sound exhausted and lonely.

alternatives.label: Earlier reckoning of Joash of Israel's reign

roles: leader of the sons of the prophets

skills.name: Ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen (a wealthy farm)

gifts.name: A double portion of Elijah's spirit

events.title: Called from the plough
events.summary: Elijah throws his cloak over him; Elisha slaughters his oxen, feeds the people and follows Elijah.

events.title: Receives Elijah's mantle
events.summary: He refuses to leave Elijah, asks for a double portion of his spirit, sees him taken up, and parts the Jordan with the fallen cloak.

events.title: Heals Jericho's water; the Bethel youths
events.summary: He purifies the spring with salt; on the road to Bethel youths mock him and two bears maul forty-two of them.

events.title: Water in the Moabite campaign
events.summary: For Jehoshaphat's sake he prophesies to the allied kings; ditches fill with water and Moab is routed.

events.title: The widow's oil
events.summary: A prophet's widow fills borrowed jars with oil to pay her debts and save her sons from slavery.

events.title: The Shunammite's son
events.summary: He promises a hospitable woman a son; when the boy dies she rides to Carmel, and Elisha raises him. Later she recovers her land.

events.title: Feeds a hundred men
events.summary: He cures a pot of poisoned stew and feeds a hundred with twenty barley loaves, with some left over.

events.title: Heals Naaman
events.summary: He tells the Aramean commander to wash seven times in the Jordan; Naaman is cleansed and confesses the God of Israel. Gehazi is struck with leprosy for greed.

events.title: Horses and chariots of fire at Dothan
events.summary: Surrounded by Aramean troops, he prays that his servant's eyes be opened, strikes the soldiers with blindness, leads them to Samaria and has them fed and released.

events.title: Siege of Samaria lifted
events.summary: During a terrible famine he predicts cheap food the next day; the Arameans flee in panic and four lepers discover the empty camp.

events.title: Hazael and Jehu
events.summary: He weeps as he tells Hazael he will be king of Aram and harm Israel; he sends a disciple to anoint Jehu, fulfilling Elijah's commission.

events.title: Death and a final miracle
events.summary: On his deathbed he has King Joash strike arrows; after burial a dead man thrown into his tomb revives on touching his bones.
