summary:
Elisha son of Shaphat was Elijah's disciple and successor, called from the plough at Abel-meholah. When Elijah was taken up, Elisha received his cloak and a double portion of his spirit, and he went on to a long ministry of about fifty years through the reigns of several northern kings.

Where Elijah was a solitary figure of confrontation, Elisha often worked among the communities of the 'sons of the prophets', and many of his miracles meet ordinary needs: a widow's debts, a poisoned pot, a lost axe-head, a childless woman, a dead son. He also acted on the international stage, advising kings in war, healing the Aramean commander Naaman, foretelling Hazael's rule in Damascus, and setting Jehu's coup in motion.

His miracles of multiplying bread and raising the dead are widely seen as anticipations of Jesus' ministry, and Jesus cites his healing of the foreigner Naaman as a sign of God's grace to the Gentiles.
textSays: Son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah, anointed to succeed Elijah (1 Kgs 19:16). Received a double portion of Elijah's spirit (2 Kgs 2:9-15). Performed many miracles (2 Kgs 2-8), anointed Jehu through a disciple (2 Kgs 9:1-3), died in the reign of Joash of Israel (2 Kgs 13:14-20). Jesus mentions Naaman's healing (Luke 4:27).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition counts sixteen miracles by Elisha against eight by Elijah, as the fulfilment of the double portion. The 'double portion' is also read as the firstborn's inheritance (Deut 21:17), marking him as Elijah's heir.

Honoured as a saint (14 June in many calendars). His miracles are read typologically: the Jordan cleansing of Naaman as baptism, the feeding of a hundred as foreshadowing the feeding of the multitudes, the raising by his bones as related to the veneration of relics.

Elisha is generally presented as a model of faithful discipleship and succession, and his miracles as signs of God's care amid apostasy. The bear episode is explained by many as judgment on a mob of young men mocking God's prophet, rather than on small children.

The Elisha cycle is usually seen as a collection of prophetic legends from northern prophetic guilds, with some stories possibly transferred between Elijah and Elisha. Scholars note its chronological placement is loose (e.g. 2 Kgs 8:1-6 after Gehazi's leprosy).

strengths: Persistent loyalty to his master (2 Kgs 2:2-6)
failures: Harsh curse on the Bethel youths is often discussed as troubling (2 Kgs 2:24)
Anger at Joash's half-hearted arrow-striking (2 Kgs 13:19)
turningPoints: Elijah's ascension and the mantle (2 Kgs 2:13-14)

context: Elisha worked during the decline of the Omride dynasty and the rise of Jehu's, when Aram-Damascus under Ben-hadad and then Hazael pressed hard on Israel. Prophetic communities ('sons of the prophets') lived at Bethel, Jericho and Gilgal.
legacy: Elisha embodies the continuity of the prophetic office. Ben Sira praises him (Sir 48:12-14, deuterocanonical). In the Gospels, Jesus' feeding miracles and raising of the widow's son at Nain echo Elisha (and Elijah), and Jesus uses Naaman to challenge Nazareth.

traditions.text: Elisha performed twice as many miracles as Elijah, sixteen to eight.
traditions.source: Later rabbinic and medieval Jewish commentary (exact source needs verification)

traditions.text: Elisha's tomb was venerated at Samaria-Sebaste, alongside that of John the Baptist, in the 4th century.
traditions.source: Jerome, Letter 108 (Epitaph of Paula); section needs verification

voice: Steady, practical and compassionate; speaks briefly, often with a touch of irony, and sees spiritual realities others miss.

roles: commander of the army of Aram

events.title: Healed in the Jordan
events.summary: On the advice of an Israelite slave girl he comes to Elisha, reluctantly dips seven times in the Jordan, is healed of his skin disease, and confesses there is no God in all the earth but in Israel.

journey.note: Commander in Aram.
Comes to the king of Israel and to Elisha's house.
Washes seven times and is cleansed.
Returns with earth from Israel to worship the LORD.

summary: Naaman was a great Aramean commander afflicted with a skin disease. Directed by a captive Israelite girl to Elisha, he was healed after humbling himself to wash in the Jordan, and he returned home to worship the God of Israel. Jesus cites him as an example of God's grace reaching foreigners.
textSays: Commander of Aram's army, a mighty man but a leper (2 Kgs 5:1). Healed by washing seven times in the Jordan (2 Kgs 5:14); asked pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon (2 Kgs 5:18). Mentioned by Jesus (Luke 4:27).
voice: Proud soldier who becomes humbled and grateful; speaks with a commander's directness.

gifts.name: Visionary prophecy of the heavenly council

events.title: Prophesies against Ahab
events.summary: Against four hundred court prophets promising victory, he foresees Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd and a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths. He is struck and imprisoned; Ahab dies as he said.

summary: Micaiah son of Imlah was the lone prophet who told Ahab the truth before the battle of Ramoth-gilead. Summoned at Jehoshaphat's request, he first mockingly echoed the court prophets, then described a vision of God's council sending a lying spirit to entice Ahab. He staked his credibility on the outcome, and Ahab died.
textSays: A prophet Ahab hated because he never prophesied good concerning him (1 Kgs 22:8). Declared he would speak only what the LORD said (1 Kgs 22:14), described the heavenly council (1 Kgs 22:19-23), and was imprisoned (1 Kgs 22:27).
voice: Ironic, unflinching and alone; speaks what he has seen regardless of the cost.

skills.name: Teaching the law through officials and Levites

events.title: Sends teachers of the law
events.summary: He removes high places and sends officials and Levites with the Book of the Law through Judah's cities.

events.title: Allies with Ahab at Ramoth-gilead
events.summary: He insists on hearing a true prophet, but joins Ahab in battle anyway and narrowly escapes; Jehu son of Hanani rebukes him.

events.title: Appoints judges
events.summary: He appoints judges in fortified cities, charging them to judge in the fear of the LORD without bribery.

events.title: Victory by praise
events.summary: Facing Moab, Ammon and Meunites, he prays, 'We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you'; singers lead the army and the enemies destroy each other.

events.title: Campaign against Moab
events.summary: With Jehoram of Israel and the king of Edom he marches through Edom; Elisha prophesies for his sake.

summary: Jehoshaphat, son of Asa, was one of Judah's better kings. He taught the law across the land, reformed the courts, and led Judah in prayer when invaded. His great weakness was alliance with the house of Ahab, including the marriage of his son Jehoram to Athaliah, which brought Baal worship and near-extinction to David's line.
textSays: Son of Asa, reigned twenty-five years (1 Kgs 22:41-42), walked in his father's ways though high places remained (1 Kgs 22:43). Made peace with Israel (1 Kgs 22:44). Chronicles details his reforms, judges and victory (2 Chr 17-20) and rebukes his alliances (2 Chr 19:2; 20:35-37). Listed in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:8).

interpretations.view: Praised as a godly reformer and cited as a model of dependence in crisis (2 Chr 20:12), but also as a warning against compromising alliances. The 'valley of Jehoshaphat' (Joel 3:2) is a symbolic name ('the LORD judges'); later tradition identified it with the Kidron Valley.

voice: Earnest, devout and agreeable; quick to ask for the LORD's word, sometimes too eager to please allies.

aliases: Jehu son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi

events.title: Anointed at Ramoth-gilead
events.summary: A disciple of Elisha anoints him privately as king and commissions him to strike Ahab's house.

events.title: Kills Joram and Ahaziah
events.summary: He drives to Jezreel, shoots Joram of Israel and throws his body on Naboth's field; Ahaziah of Judah is also killed.

events.title: Jezebel's death
events.summary: He orders her thrown from a window.

events.title: Destroys Ahab's house and Baal's worshippers
events.summary: He has Ahab's seventy sons killed, then gathers Baal's worshippers in their temple in Samaria and slaughters them.

events.title: Keeps Jeroboam's calves
events.summary: He does not turn from the golden calves; Hazael begins to cut off Israel's territory.

summary: Jehu, a commander in Israel's army, was anointed at Elisha's instruction to wipe out the house of Ahab. His bloody coup killed two kings, Jezebel and Ahab's descendants, and he exterminated Baal worship in Israel. God commends his zeal with a dynasty of four generations, yet he kept Jeroboam's calves, and Hosea later condemns the bloodshed of Jezreel.
textSays: Anointed king of Israel (2 Kgs 9:6), killed Joram, Ahaziah, Jezebel and Ahab's house (2 Kgs 9-10), destroyed Baal worship (2 Kgs 10:28), but did not turn from Jeroboam's sins (2 Kgs 10:29-31). Reigned twenty-eight years (2 Kgs 10:36). Hosea announces punishment for 'the blood of Jezreel' on his house (Hos 1:4).

interpretations.view: Readers have long debated how to reconcile God's commendation (2 Kgs 10:30) with Hosea's condemnation (Hos 1:4). Many explain that Jehu carried out a commanded judgment but with excessive and self-serving violence; others think Hosea's word condemns his house's later failure rather than the coup itself.

The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (c. 841 BC) shows a king of Israel bowing with tribute, labelled as Jehu 'son of Omri' (meaning of the Omride land), widely accepted as the only surviving image of an Israelite king. The Tel Dan stele's claim that an Aramean king killed Joram and Ahaziah suggests rival accounts of the same events.

voice: Brash, fast and violent; speaks with mocking bravado and boasts of his zeal for the LORD.

nation: Israel by birth; queen of Judah

events.title: Seizes the throne of Judah
events.summary: After her son Ahaziah is killed by Jehu, she destroys the royal family; only the infant Joash is hidden in the temple.

events.title: Overthrown and killed
events.summary: In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada crowns Joash; crying 'Treason!', she is taken out and killed.

summary: Athaliah, of Ahab's house and wife of King Jehoram of Judah, was the only woman to rule Judah or Israel as monarch in the Bible. After her son's death she tried to wipe out David's line and ruled six years, promoting Baal worship, until the priest Jehoiada crowned the hidden child Joash and she was executed.
textSays: Called daughter of Ahab (2 Kgs 8:18) and daughter (granddaughter) of Omri (2 Kgs 8:26). Mother of Ahaziah; destroyed the royal offspring and reigned six years (2 Kgs 11:1-3). Her sons broke into the temple for the Baals (2 Chr 24:7).

interpretations.view: Whether she was Ahab's daughter (and possibly Jezebel's) or Omri's daughter, Ahab's sister, is debated; most take 'daughter of Omri' as 'of the house of Omri'.

voice: Ruthless and commanding; speaks with the entitlement of a dynasty that will not yield power.

events.title: Hidden and crowned at seven
events.summary: Rescued from Athaliah's massacre by his aunt Jehosheba, hidden six years in the temple, and crowned by Jehoiada.

events.title: Repairs the temple
events.summary: He sets up a chest for offerings to pay workers to repair the temple.

events.title: Apostasy and Zechariah's murder
events.summary: After Jehoiada's death he turns to idols and has Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned in the temple court.

events.title: Pays off Hazael; assassinated
events.summary: He gives temple treasures to Hazael of Aram and is killed by his own servants.

summary: Joash, the infant survivor of Athaliah's purge, was made king of Judah at seven by the priest Jehoiada. While Jehoiada lived he did right and restored the temple, but afterwards he turned to idols and had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned. He paid tribute to Hazael of Aram and was assassinated after a forty-year reign.
textSays: Son of Ahaziah, hidden by Jehosheba (2 Kgs 11:2), crowned at seven (2 Kgs 11:21), did right all the days Jehoiada instructed him (2 Kgs 12:2), repaired the temple, later killed Zechariah (2 Chr 24:20-22) and was assassinated (2 Kgs 12:20-21).

interpretations.view: Many identify the Zechariah of Matt 23:35 and Luke 11:51 with Zechariah son of Jehoiada, the last murder in the Hebrew canon's order (Chronicles last); Matthew's 'son of Barachiah' raises a debated identification with the prophet Zechariah (Zech 1:1).

voice: Dutiful while guided, later defensive and resentful; speaks like a king who never learned to stand on his own.
